prompt: Why does a sparse table use more than one linear array of summaries?

options.text: It stores only the original values, with no extra summaries.
options.explanation: Those values are just its first row.

options.text: Each element is copied exactly twice.
options.explanation: It has a separate row for every fitting power-of-two block length.

options.text: It stores a row of fitting blocks at each power-of-two length.
options.explanation: Correct. Logarithmically many rows with up to n entries each give O(n log n) storage for n input elements.

options.text: It stores a separate entry for every possible pair of endpoints.
options.explanation: That is the quadratic every-range table, not a sparse table.

workedExample: Start with one-element blocks. Each next row doubles block length and stores every starting position where that block fits. There are logarithmically many rows, each of at most linear size. This preprocessing and memory buy constant-time overlap queries for idempotent operations on unchanged data.

prompt: A trading system holds the last 10 million prices in an array, answers about 50,000 range-minimum queries per second, and also overwrites individual prices about 1,000 times per second. Which structure fits best?

options.text: A sparse table, for its O(1) queries
options.explanation: With n the number of prices, a point change can affect O(n) stored blocks across levels, whereas a segment tree updates O(log n) nodes.
Correct. O(log n) tree work, with n the number of prices, for queries and point updates supports both operation types; throughput still needs benchmarking, and the structure stays O(n) in memory.

options.text: A plain array, scanning each range
options.explanation: Wide ranges require scanning many prices for every query. A range-summary structure avoids that repeated work.
Prefix minima only answer ranges that start at index 0. min has no inverse, so you cannot subtract two prefixes to get a general range.

workedExample: The workload has both queries and frequent changes. Sparse-table queries are fast, but one changed price can affect many overlapping stored blocks. A segment tree changes one node per level and answers ranges with logarithmically many pieces, using linear memory. Here n counts prices. Benchmark the implementation to establish throughput; asymptotic bounds alone do not prove that a requested rate is achievable.
